lessonTitle: Pool Boiling and the Critical Heat Flux

blocks.text: A nuclear fuel rod, a kettle element and a steam boiler tube all boil water at their surfaces, and all can be destroyed if the heat flux is pushed a little too high. The danger is not that boiling stops but that it changes character so abruptly that the metal temperature can jump by hundreds of kelvin in a second.

blocks.markdown: In **pool boiling** a heated surface is submerged in a stagnant liquid, and fluid motion is due to buoyancy and to bubble growth and departure. The heat flux depends on the **excess temperature** $\Delta T_e=T_s-T_{sat}$ (K), the wall temperature above the saturation temperature of the liquid. Plotting $q''_s$ against $\Delta T_e$ gives the **boiling curve**, which shows distinct regimes.

blocks.title: Boiling curve and excess temperature
blocks.text: $\Delta T_e=T_s-T_{sat}$. The boiling curve shows the surface heat flux $q''_s$ against $\Delta T_e$ on logarithmic axes. Its peak is the **critical heat flux** (CHF), $q''_{max}$, and its first minimum is the Leidenfrost point $q''_{min}$.

rows: Liquid superheated slightly; heat leaves by free convection to the surface, evaporating at the free surface
Bubbles form at nucleation sites, depart and stir the liquid; very effective
Rises steeply up to the CHF
Unstable partial vapour film forms and collapses repeatedly
Stable vapour blanket separates the liquid from the surface; radiation becomes important
Rises slowly again; coefficient is low
blocks.caption: Pool boiling regimes for saturated water at atmospheric pressure (values typical, boundaries approximate)

blocks.markdown: The excess temperature ranges are typical for water; they shift with pressure, surface finish and fluid. Within nucleate boiling the heat transfer coefficient is exceptionally high (about $10^4$ W/m$^2$K and above) because bubble departure drags cool liquid onto the surface. The curve peaks at the **critical heat flux**, beyond which vapour production is so rapid that vapour columns merge into a film and liquid cannot reach the surface.

blocks.caption: Zuber (hydrodynamic instability) estimate of the critical heat flux for saturated pool boiling on a large horizontal surface; h_fg latent heat (J/kg), sigma surface tension (N/m), rho_l and rho_v the liquid and vapour densities (kg/m^3), g gravity (m/s^2)

blocks.title: Critical heat flux of water at atmospheric pressure
blocks.prompt: Estimate the critical heat flux for saturated pool boiling of water at 1 atm (100 $^\circ$C) on a large horizontal surface. Typical saturated properties: $\rho_l=957.9$ kg/m$^3$, $\rho_v=0.5956$ kg/m$^3$, $h_{fg}=2.257\times10^6$ J/kg, $\sigma=0.0589$ N/m.

steps.text: Zuber's hydrodynamic-stability result gives the maximum heat flux at which liquid can still rewet the surface: $q''_{max}=0.131\,h_{fg}\rho_v^{1/2}[\sigma g(\rho_l-\rho_v)]^{1/4}$.
Evaluate the bracket: $\sigma g(\rho_l-\rho_v)=0.0589\times9.81\times(957.9-0.5956)=553.1$ in SI units, and its fourth root is $4.8496$.

blocks.answer: $q''_{max}\approx1.11$ MW/m$^2$. This is the order of magnitude, about 1 MW/m$^2$, for water at atmospheric pressure.

blocks.markdown: The CHF increases with latent heat and vapour density and with surface tension: strongly with $\rho_v^{1/2}$ (so with pressure) and weakly with the fourth root of $\sigma g(\rho_l-\rho_v)$. It is independent of the wall material. The equation uses properties at saturation.

blocks.title: Will the heater burn out?
blocks.prompt: An electrical plate heater of area 0.04 m$^2$ is submerged in saturated water at 1 atm. Using $q''_{max}\approx1.11$ MW/m$^2$ from the previous example, decide whether burnout is expected when the electrical power is (a) 20 kW and (b) 60 kW, and find a safe maximum power with a 30% margin.

steps.text: The heater supplies a fixed power, so the surface heat flux is $q''=P/A$ and it is set by the electrical input, not by the surface temperature. This is a heat-flux-controlled surface.
(a) $q''=20000/0.04=0.50$ MW/m$^2$, which is 45% of the critical value. This is in the nucleate boiling range and is safe.

(b) $q''=60000/0.04=1.50$ MW/m$^2$, which is 136% of the critical value and exceeds it. The surface cannot stay in nucleate boiling; vapour blankets it and the temperature jumps to film boiling, possibly melting the heater.
Safe limit with a 30% margin: $P_{safe}=0.7\,q''_{max}A=0.7\times1.107e+06\times0.04=31.0$ kW.

blocks.answer: (a) safe; (b) burnout, since 1.50 MW/m$^2$ exceeds 1.11 MW/m$^2$; safe power about 31 kW.

blocks.markdown: Why does burnout occur? In a **heat-flux-controlled** system (an electrical heater, a nuclear reactor) the engineer sets $q''$ and the surface temperature adjusts. If $q''$ exceeds $q''_{max}$, nucleate boiling cannot carry it; the system moves to film boiling, where the coefficient is far lower, so to carry the same flux the surface temperature must jump to a very high value. This is called burnout or boiling crisis. In a **temperature-controlled** system (for example steam condensing on the other side of the wall) the surface temperature is set, and the heat flux simply falls when $\Delta T_e$ passes the peak.

items: Identify the regime from $\Delta T_e$ (or from the described bubble behaviour).
For saturated pool boiling estimate $q''_{max}$ with Zuber's equation using saturated properties.
Compute the actual flux $q''=P/A$ for a heater.
Compare with $q''_{max}$ and apply a safety margin; heat-flux-controlled surfaces must stay well below it.

blocks.title: Heat-flux-controlled surfaces
blocks.text: The danger is the abrupt jump. Beyond $q''_{max}$ the surface temperature may rise by several hundred kelvin to reach film boiling, above the melting point of many heater materials. Reducing the power after burnout will not restore nucleate boiling until the flux falls below the Leidenfrost flux, which is much lower than the CHF.

blocks.title: Where the peak matters
blocks.text: The CHF is the design limit for boilers, reactors and electronics cooling with boiling. A design must keep the operating heat flux well below $q''_{max}$ (typically a margin of 20% to 50%).

points: The boiling curve has four regimes: natural convection, nucleate, transition and film boiling, with the CHF at the peak of nucleate boiling.
Zuber: $q''_{max}=0.131h_{fg}\rho_v^{1/2}[\sigma g(\rho_l-\rho_v)]^{1/4}$, about $1.1$ to $1.3$ MW/m$^2$ for water at 1 atm.
In a heat-flux-controlled surface, exceeding the CHF forces a jump to film boiling and a large wall temperature rise (burnout).
Keep the operating flux with a safety margin below the CHF.

questions.stem: Arrange the pool boiling regimes in the order met when the surface excess temperature $\Delta T_e$ is slowly increased from a small value.

options.text: Nucleate, natural convection, film, transition boiling
Natural convection, nucleate, transition, film boiling
Natural convection, transition, nucleate, film boiling
Film, transition, nucleate, natural convection boiling

questions.correctOptionText: Natural convection, nucleate, transition, film boiling

distractorRationale.a: Natural convection boiling occurs first, at the smallest $\Delta T_e$.
distractorRationale.c: Transition boiling comes after the nucleate peak, not before it.
distractorRationale.d: This is the reverse order of increasing $\Delta T_e$ for a heat-flux curve and puts film boiling first.

questions.explanation: At small excess temperature there are no bubbles and heat leaves by free convection. Bubbles then form (nucleate), the vapour film is unstable (transition) and finally stable (film boiling).

questions.stem: Water at 1 atm is boiled on a plate whose surface is 15 K above the saturation temperature, with discrete bubbles forming at points on the surface and rising. The regime is

distractorRationale.a: This has no bubbles at the surface; it occurs at $\Delta T_e$ below about 5 K.
distractorRationale.b: This involves a partial, unstable vapour film at $\Delta T_e$ of roughly 30 to 120 K.
distractorRationale.c: This needs a stable vapour blanket at $\Delta T_e$ above about 120 K.

questions.explanation: Isolated bubbles at nucleation sites with $\Delta T_e$ between about 5 K and 30 K characterise nucleate boiling, the regime with the highest heat transfer coefficients and the CHF at its upper end.

questions.stem: Estimate the critical heat flux for saturated liquid nitrogen at 1 atm on a large horizontal surface using Zuber's equation with typical properties $\rho_l=807$ kg/m$^3$, $\rho_v=4.6$ kg/m$^3$, $h_{fg}=1.99\times10^5$ J/kg and $\sigma=0.0088$ N/m. Give the answer in kW/m$^2$.
questions.explanation: $q''_{max}=0.131\times1.99\times10^5\times\sqrt{4.6}\times[0.0088\times9.81\times(807-4.6)]^{1/4}$. The vapour term is $2.1448$ and the bracket is $69.270$ with fourth root $2.8849$, giving 161302 W/m$^2$ $=161$ kW/m$^2$. The CHF is well below that of water because $h_{fg}$ and $\sigma$ are much smaller.

questions.stem: Using the water properties $\rho_l=957.9$ kg/m$^3$, $\rho_v=0.5956$ kg/m$^3$, $h_{fg}=2.257\times10^6$ J/kg, $\sigma=0.0589$ N/m, estimate the critical heat flux of saturated water boiling on a large horizontal plate on the Moon, where $g=1.62$ m/s$^2$. Give the answer in MW/m$^2$.

The CHF of a plate heater in a particular boiling liquid is 1.1 MW/m$^2$. The plate has area 0.05 m$^2$ and is heated electrically. For a safety margin the heater is to run at no more than 70% of the CHF. Find the maximum electrical power in kW.
questions.explanation: The surface heat flux is $q''=P/A$. The limit is $q''=0.7\times1.1\times10^6=770000$ W/m$^2$, so $P_{max}=0.77\times10^6\times0.05=38500$ W $=38.5$ kW. Power above this erodes the margin to burnout.

questions.stem: For an electrically heated wire submerged in water, the heat flux is increased gradually past the critical heat flux. What happens?

options.text: The wire temperature jumps sharply to a film boiling value, and it may melt
The heat flux falls along the transition curve to a lower wire temperature
The wire temperature rises slowly and smoothly along the nucleate curve
Nothing changes since the water is always cooling the wire

questions.correctOptionText: The wire temperature jumps sharply to a film boiling value, and it may melt

distractorRationale.b: This is only possible if the surface temperature (not flux) is controlled.
distractorRationale.c: Nucleate boiling cannot carry flux above the CHF.
distractorRationale.d: Above the CHF vapour blankets the surface and cooling degrades suddenly.

questions.explanation: At a fixed power the heater has no stable nucleate state above the CHF, so the surface temperature jumps to the film boiling branch at the same heat flux. That temperature is far higher, which can melt the wire.

questions.stem: In which boiling regime does the heat flux decrease as the excess temperature increases?

options.text: Film boiling at very high $\Delta T_e$

distractorRationale.a: In nucleate boiling the flux rises rapidly with $\Delta T_e$.
distractorRationale.b: The flux rises slowly with $\Delta T_e$.
distractorRationale.d: Film boiling flux generally rises with $\Delta T_e$, due to radiation and conduction in the film.

questions.explanation: In transition boiling more of the surface is blanketed by vapour as $\Delta T_e$ rises, so the average heat flux decreases from the CHF to the Leidenfrost minimum.

questions.stem: Describe the four regimes of the pool boiling curve for water at atmospheric pressure. For each give the approximate range of excess temperature and the mechanism of heat transfer, and mark the critical heat flux and the Leidenfrost point on your description.
markingGuide: Natural convection boiling: $\Delta T_e<\approx5$ K, free convection, no bubble formation at the surface.
Nucleate boiling: about 5 K to 30 K; isolated bubbles then jets and columns; very high $h$; the CHF is at the end of this regime.
Transition boiling: about 30 K to 120 K; unstable vapour film, flux falls with $\Delta T_e$; the Leidenfrost point is the minimum at its end.
Film boiling: above about 120 K; stable vapour blanket, low $h$, radiation matters.
questions.explanation: A complete answer states the mechanism and the trend of $q''$ with $\Delta T_e$ in each regime and locates the maximum and minimum of the curve.

questions.stem: Contrast heat-flux-controlled and temperature-controlled heating. Explain why a nuclear fuel rod or an electrical heater is vulnerable to burnout at the CHF while a surface heated by condensing steam is not, and describe two design practices to avoid burnout.
markingGuide: Heat-flux-controlled: the energy input fixes $q''$, and the surface temperature adjusts to whatever is needed to transfer it.
At $q''>q''_{max}$ no nucleate boiling state exists, so the surface jumps to film boiling where $h$ is low and the wall temperature becomes very large (burnout).
Temperature-controlled (condensing steam): the surface temperature is set, so beyond the peak the flux simply falls along the transition curve with no runaway.
Designs: keep $q''$ well below $q''_{max}$ with a margin; raise $q''_{max}$ by increasing pressure or using subcooled liquid or enhanced surfaces; or use controls that trip the power.
questions.explanation: The distinction is the control variable. Only a flux-controlled surface can pass the peak with no flux-limiting feedback, which causes the discontinuous jump in temperature.

questions.stem: A surfactant lowers the surface tension of saturated water by 30% (to 70% of its original value). All other properties are unchanged. Using Zuber's equation, find the ratio of the new critical heat flux to the original. Give a dimensionless number.
questions.explanation: Zuber's CHF scales as $\sigma^{1/4}$. The ratio is $0.7^{1/4}=0.9147$, so the CHF falls by about 8.5%. A weak dependence on $\sigma$ means large property changes give small CHF changes.
